first.rationale: The two live regressions are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and the inherited record points at onboarding/signup friction as the lever that moved exactly those metrics (memory_86, memory_31), with activation messaging (memory_91) as the close second. Promotional pricing is the tempting response to the competitor, but memory_73 explicitly records a 30-day retention hit and warns against generalizing it — against a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective that is the wrong trade, so I am deliberately not spending the single slot there. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are sound but address neither regression this week. I am spending verification on memory_86 and memory_31 because they are the two memories actually load-bearing for the action I intend, and both are consolidated summaries whose original records I have not seen: I want to know whether the 'durable lift' in memory_31 was measured past week one, whether either was SMB-only or ran during a period confounded by other changes, and whether the onboarding win came from removing steps or merely reordering them. Downstream value risk: stripping signup fields and onboarding steps can shift cost onto later stages — thinner qualification data, worse routing, and possible degradation of the enterprise demo-request path in memory_44 — so completion lift alone must not be the success criterion. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: the underlying evidence is aged (day 12 and day 52) and the market has changed since, so I want a held-out control and 30-day retention plus downstream qualified-pipeline as guardrail metrics, not just completion rate. If verification shows memory_31's lift was week-one-only or confounded, I would shift the slot to activation_messaging (memory_91), which targets the larger regression.

mid.rationale: Verification supported the intended action and sharpened which version of it to run. exp_86 (shortened onboarding flow) is the cleanest record available: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and critically 30-day retention +3% — it improves the guardrail rather than trading against it, which is exactly what the sustainable-long-term-qualified-revenue objective demands. exp_31 also confirmed, but with two caveats I am carrying forward rather than discarding: retention was -1% and the result explicitly did not replicate outside SMB. So I run the onboarding-shortening variant as the primary intervention and treat signup-field removal as a secondary, SMB-scoped arm at most — I will not bundle aggressive field-stripping into a cross-segment rollout on the strength of a result that is stated not to generalize. Against the competitor's entry pricing, promotional_pricing remains the wrong use of the single slot: memory_73 records a material 30-day retention hit and an explicit warning not to generalize it, and buying price-sensitive SMB accounts that churn does not produce sustainable qualified revenue. Onboarding is also the more defensible competitive answer, since time-to-value is a durable differentiator whereas a discount is immediately matchable. activation_messaging (memory_91) targets the larger regression (-6%) and is my named fallback, but it went unverified and onboarding completion is plausibly upstream of activation, so the onboarding fix may recover part of the activation gap on its own. Downstream value risk stands: shortening onboarding can push cost into later stages via thinner qualification data and worse routing, and could degrade the enterprise demo-request path in memory_44, which was never tested under a shortened flow. Guardrails are therefore 30-day retention, downstream qualified pipeline, and enterprise conversion — not completion rate alone. Standard experiment with a held-out control rather than broad rollout: exp_86 is 24 days old, predates the competitor's launch and the current regressions, and confirmation of a past result is not proof it holds in changed market conditions. If retention or enterprise pipeline moves against us, I stop and shift the next slot to activation_messaging.

final2.rationale: The news is urgent but it is not new evidence about what works. Nothing in the last three days changed the underlying record: exp_86 remains the only verified intervention that lifts completion (+13%), cuts time-to-value (-2.1 days) and improves 30-day retention (+3%) at the same time, and memory_73 still records that promotional pricing materially damaged 30-day retention with an explicit warning not to generalize it. Escalating competitive pressure raises the cost of being wrong; it does not raise the probability that the discount works. I hold simplify_onboarding as the single experiment. Two further reasons to resist the pricing pivot specifically. First, memory_73 describes promotional pricing as an acquisition response for price-sensitive SMB; using it as a churn-defense instrument against accounts already in save conversations is an extrapolation beyond what that record supports, and it is exactly the kind of stretch that urgency makes feel justified. Second, matching a competitor's discount in a market where they have just cut twice invites a third cut — we would be buying retention of the least durable accounts at the price of the retention metric the objective is defined by. Discounting also anchors expectations in the installed base and is very hard to unwind, which is a downstream cost that would not show up in this cycle's numbers. The honest framing for leadership: a pricing/retention response to the competitor is a commercial decision that may well be warranted, but it is not this week's growth experiment and it should not be smuggled in under evidence that does not support it. If leadership elects to discount, it should be scoped as a narrow, time-boxed save offer to already-churning SMB accounts, measured on 30-day retention, and owned separately — not funded from this slot and not justified by memory_73. Carried-forward caveats stand: exp_31's signup-field result was SMB-only and cost 1% retention, so field-stripping stays a secondary SMB-scoped arm at most; exp_86 predates both the competitor launch and the current regressions, so it runs with a held-out control. Guardrails remain 30-day retention, downstream qualified pipeline, and the enterprise demo-request path in memory_44, which was never tested under a shortened flow. activation_messaging (memory_91) remains the unverified fallback for the -6% activation gap if onboarding does not recover it.
